report.answer_text:
2025 had five Starship flights, flights 7 through 11. The first three ended in failure, and the last two succeeded.
Flights 7, 8 and 9 (January to May): three failures in a row
Starship suffered explosive failures in three back-to-back test flights before its successful 10th flight on August 26.[1]
Flight 7 was in January and flight 8 in March. From my own knowledge rather than the search results, both ships were lost during ascent, and the booster was caught by the tower arms on at least one of them.
Flight 9 launched in late May. It flew farther than the previous two attempts, which ended in explosive failure.[2] The booster made a controlled splashdown in the Gulf of Mexico and skipped the tower "catch" attempt.[2] The ship's payload bay door failed to open on that flight.[3]
Before flight 10, engineers fixed a part called the fuel diffuser, which may have caused a pressure problem in the nose cone.[4]
Flight 10 (August 26): the turnaround
The launch was two days late, and it appeared to be a remarkably successful test after the three back-to-back failures.[5]
The upper stage flew into a sub-orbital trajectory as planned, which the three previous flights had failed to do.[5]
This time the payload door opened.[3] The ship re-ignited an engine in space and made a soft splashdown in the Indian Ocean.[6] The Super Heavy booster made a controlled splashdown in the Gulf of Mexico.[6]
Flight 11 (October 13): the last Version 2 flight
Starship made it halfway around the world and released mock satellites, as it had on flight 10.[7] It carried eight mock Starlink satellites.[7]
SpaceX ran a series of tests during the ship's entry over the Indian Ocean, as practice for future landings back at the launch site.[7]
The heat shield had patches of reconfigured tiles, and some tiles were deliberately left out to test how well the ship tolerates losing them.[1]
The booster's return burn went from 13 engines to five and then three, a rehearsal for the next-generation booster's landing maneuvers.[1]
It was the last flight of the current Version 2 design.[8]
What came next
The next-generation booster and a new ship version were slated to begin test flights in 2026, both with improved Raptor engines.[1] NASA is counting on a modified Starship to land two astronauts on the Moon as early as 2027.[5]
